title: Technical Writing
description: How to write documentation that people can use: knowing the reader, choosing the kind of page, writing clear sentences, procedures and reference entries, documenting an API, and testing the result.
audience: A capable adult who writes emails and reports well enough and now has to explain a product, process or system to people who did not build it. Engineers, analysts, support staff and career-changers. No documentation tools are assumed; a few lessons read short HTTP, JSON or Markdown snippets.
outcomes: You'll be able to say who a page is for, what they are trying to do, and what they already know.
You'll be able to choose between a tutorial, a how-to guide, a reference page and an explanation, and say why mixing them fails.
You'll be able to turn a passive, vague sentence into a clear one, and measure the change.
You'll be able to write a procedure with one action per step, and a reference entry with every field a reader needs.
You'll be able to document an HTTP API endpoint with its request, response and errors, and test the page with a reader.

sources.title: Google Technical Writing courses (Technical Writing One and Two)
Diátaxis: a systematic approach to technical documentation (Daniele Procida)
GOV.UK content design: planning, writing and managing content
RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics (status codes)

modules.summary: Audience, the four kinds of page, and the structure that lets a reader find things.

modules.title: Clear sentences
modules.summary: Words, sentences and editing, with ways to measure what you changed.

lessons.title: Who is reading, and why
lessons.objective: State a page's reader, goal and starting knowledge in one sentence, and recognise the curse of knowledge.

concepts.title: Audience
concepts.summary: The people who will read a page, defined by what they want to do and what they already know.

concepts.title: Curse of knowledge
concepts.summary: Once you know something it is hard to imagine not knowing it, so you skip steps a newcomer needs.

concepts.title: Reader goal
concepts.summary: The task the reader is trying to finish, which the page exists to serve.

misconceptions: Learners write for 'everyone', and so for nobody; a page needs one primary reader, and others can be signposted.
Learners think experts want less explanation; experts want less about the basics but still need the exact details.
sequence: Ask what happens when an engineer writes setup instructions for a colleague who has never seen the system.
Tell the tapping study: in 1990 Elizabeth Newton asked tappers to tap the rhythm of a well-known song; they predicted listeners would name it half the time, and 3 of 120 did.
Define audience, goal and starting knowledge, and write a one-sentence statement.
Find the skipped steps in a short paragraph that assumes a terminal is already open.
Handle mixed audiences by layering or linking.
examples: Audience statement: 'A developer who has used a REST API before, wants to send their first authenticated request, and has not yet created a key.'
Newton's study: 3 of 120 is 2.5%, against a prediction of 50%.

figures.shows: Three pages with their readers, goals and starting knowledge, one row left empty.
figures.learnerAction: Complete the empty row from the paragraph shown.

questionPlan.sample: In Newton's tapping study, 3 of 120 listeners named the song. What percentage is that?
Which is the best audience statement?
choices: A support agent who has never used the admin console and needs to reset a customer's password
questionPlan.answer: A support agent who has never used the admin console and needs to reset a customer's password

questionPlan.sample: The difficulty of imagining not knowing what you know is called the curse of ___.

historyNotes: Elizabeth Newton's tapping study was her 1990 Stanford doctoral work; it was popularised by Chip and Dan Heath in Made to Stick (2007) (verify).

lessons.title: Four kinds of page
lessons.objective: Classify a page as tutorial, how-to guide, reference or explanation, and explain what goes wrong when a page mixes them.

concepts.title: Tutorial
concepts.summary: A guided lesson that takes a beginner through a project to build skill and confidence.

concepts.title: How-to guide
concepts.summary: Steps for a reader who already knows the basics to reach a specific goal.

concepts.title: Reference
concepts.summary: Accurate, complete, neutral description of a thing's parts, looked up rather than read through.

concepts.title: Explanation
concepts.summary: Discussion of why something is as it is, to deepen understanding.

misconceptions: Learners think one long page serving everyone is friendlier; the four kinds serve different needs, and a reader hunting a parameter does not want a tutorial around it.
Learners confuse tutorial and how-to; a tutorial teaches by doing a guided project, a how-to assumes skill and serves a goal.
sequence: Describe four readers: a newcomer, someone mid-task, someone checking a detail, someone asking why.
Name the four page types as the Diátaxis framework does, crediting it.
Show a mixed page and split it.
Say what each type leaves out on purpose: reference omits instruction, tutorial omits options.
examples: 'Reset a user's password' is a how-to; 'Build your first dashboard' is a tutorial; 'Password policy fields' is reference; 'Why passwords expire' is explanation.

figures.shows: Four page snippets drawn as SVG.
figures.learnerAction: Label each snippet with its type.

figures.shows: A two-axis map: study versus work, doing versus knowing, placing the four types in quadrants.

questionPlan.sample: A page lists every parameter of a function with its type and default. It is:
A page called 'Why we use eventual consistency' is:
A how-to page keeps pausing for two paragraphs of background. What is the best fix?
choices: Move the background to an explanation page and link to it
questionPlan.answer: Move the background to an explanation page and link to it

lessons.title: Structure for finding things
lessons.objective: Structure a page so a reader can find the answer by scanning: headings, front-loading, lists and tables.

concepts.title: Front-loading
concepts.summary: Put the main point or action at the start of the page, section or sentence.

concepts.title: Heading outline
concepts.summary: Headings that form a hierarchy a reader can scan and a tool can turn into a contents list.

concepts.title: Lists and tables
concepts.summary: Numbered lists for sequences, bulleted lists for sets, tables for items that share several attributes.

misconceptions: Learners write clever headings; a heading should name the content so a reader scanning gets the answer.
Learners turn everything into bullets; a connected explanation read as bullets loses the reasoning.
sequence: Readers scan in an F-shape; show a page and ask where the answer is.
Inverted pyramid: lead with the conclusion.
Headings as a task outline: verbs for procedures, nouns for reference.
Numbered, bulleted or table.
Short paragraphs, one topic each.
examples: Heading 'Configure the proxy' (a task) against 'Things to know' (empty).
Three options with a name, cost and limit each belong in a table of three columns.

figures.shows: The same content drawn as a wall of text and as a structured page, switchable.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle views and find a stated answer in each.

questionPlan.sample: Steps that must be done in order should be:
Which is the clearest heading for a procedure page?
Five plans, each with a price, a user limit and a storage limit, belong in:

lessons.title: Clear words
lessons.objective: Rewrite passive, vague or inconsistent sentences using active voice, specific verbs and one term per concept.

concepts.title: Active voice
concepts.summary: A sentence in which the actor is the subject, so the reader knows who or what does the action.

concepts.title: Consistent terminology
concepts.summary: One name for one thing throughout, because a new word suggests a new thing.

concepts.title: Ambiguous pronoun
concepts.summary: A pronoun such as it or this that could point to more than one earlier item.

misconceptions: Learners think passive is always wrong; it is right when the actor is unknown or unimportant, as in 'The file is deleted after 30 days'.
Learners vary words for elegance ('folder', then 'directory', then 'location'); in documentation the reader will assume three things.
sequence: Take 'The configuration file should be edited' and ask who edits it.
Active voice and when passive is fine.
Specific verbs over 'perform' and 'utilize'.
Consistent terms: pick a name and keep it.
Pronouns: replace this with the noun.
examples: 'The file is saved by the application' becomes 'The application saves the file'.
'Click the button. This starts the build.' becomes 'Click Build. The build starts a new container.'

figures.shows: Before and after pairs for ten sentences, with the 'after' column hidden for the learner to fill.
figures.learnerAction: Choose the best rewrite from three.

questionPlan.sample: Which is the active-voice version of 'The request is validated by the server'?
choices: The server is validating the request.

questionPlan.sample: In 'The script reads the config and writes the log. It fails if missing', what is the problem?
choices: Ambiguous pronoun: it could be the script, config or log
questionPlan.answer: Ambiguous pronoun: it could be the script, config or log

questionPlan.sample: Using one name for one thing throughout a document is called consistent ___.

lessons.title: Sentences, paragraphs and readability
lessons.objective: Shorten and untangle sentences, give each paragraph one topic, and compute a Flesch reading ease score.

concepts.title: One idea per sentence
concepts.summary: A sentence that carries a single idea is easier to read and to test.

concepts.title: Parallel structure
concepts.summary: List items that begin with the same grammatical form read as a set.

concepts.title: Flesch reading ease
concepts.summary: 206.835 − 1.015 × (words per sentence) − 84.6 × (syllables per word); higher is easier.

misconceptions: Learners treat readability scores as a quality target; a score measures sentence and word length only, and a short, wrong sentence scores well.
Learners think shortest is best; a string of very short sentences loses the connections between ideas.
sequence: A 52-word sentence with three conditions; split it.
Put conditions before actions: 'To update, open the menu'.
Parallel lists.
Flesch formula and a worked case.
What the score cannot see: accuracy, order, jargon the formula counts as long words.
examples: 15 words per sentence and 1.5 syllables per word: 206.835 − 15.225 − 126.9 = 64.71.
15 words per sentence and 1.4 syllables per word: 206.835 − 15.225 − 118.44 = 73.17.

figures.shows: Flesch calculator taking words per sentence and syllables per word.
figures.learnerAction: Enter values and read the score.

questionPlan.sample: A text averages 15 words per sentence and 1.5 syllables per word. What is its Flesch reading ease, to the nearest whole number? (206.835 − 1.015 × W − 84.6 × S)
A text averages 15 words per sentence and 1.4 syllables per word. What is the score, to the nearest whole number?
Which list is parallel?
choices: Install the package; configuring the file; run the server
Install the package; configure the file; run the server
questionPlan.answer: Install the package; configure the file; run the server

historyNotes: Rudolf Flesch published the Reading Ease formula in 1948; the coefficients above are those of his 1948 formula.

lessons.title: Editing a draft
lessons.objective: Edit a draft in separate passes for structure, sentences and words, and measure the cut.

concepts.title: Editing passes
concepts.summary: Separate passes for content, structure, sentence clarity and then correctness of words and punctuation.

concepts.title: Filler
concepts.summary: Words that carry nothing, such as 'in order to', 'it should be noted that' and 'very'.

concepts.title: Reading aloud
concepts.summary: Voicing a draft exposes tangled sentences and missing steps.

misconceptions: Learners edit everything at once and miss structural faults while fixing commas.
Learners cut words that carried a warning or a number; edits must preserve facts.
sequence: Let the draft rest before editing it.
Pass 1: what must the reader do or know; delete the rest.
Pass 2: order and headings.
Pass 3: sentences and words, using the earlier lessons.
Pass 4: check names, numbers, links.
Measure: words before and after.
examples: 'In order to start the server, it is necessary that you run the following command' (15 words) becomes 'To start the server, run this command' (7 words), a cut of 8 words, about 53%.
A 40-word paragraph edited to 28 words is a cut of 12 words, 30%.

figures.shows: A paragraph with filler highlighted and word counts per version.
figures.learnerAction: Select words to delete and see the count change.

questionPlan.sample: A paragraph is cut from 40 words to 28. What percentage was removed?
Which cut changes the meaning and should be refused?
Recall: name the four passes in order.
questionPlan.answer: Content, structure, sentences and words, then checking facts and details.

lessons.title: Writing a procedure
lessons.objective: Write a procedure with prerequisites first, one action per numbered step, and the expected result.

concepts.title: One action per step
concepts.summary: Each numbered step asks for one action, so the reader can do it, check it and place themselves in the list.

concepts.title: Prerequisites
concepts.summary: What the reader needs before step 1: access, tools, versions.

concepts.title: Expected result
concepts.summary: What the reader should see after a step or at the end, so they know it worked.

misconceptions: Learners pack several actions into one step to keep the list short; if one fails the reader cannot tell which.
Learners put the location after the action ('Click Save in the File menu'); locate first: 'In the File menu, click Save'.
sequence: Take one badly written step ('Open Settings, select Network, and click Reset').
Split into steps; each begins with an imperative verb.
Put the where before the what.
State the result and give a way to verify.
Prerequisites before the steps; troubleshooting after.
examples: 'Open Settings, select Network, and click Reset.' becomes three steps: 1. Open Settings. 2. Select Network. 3. Click Reset.
'Click Save in the File menu' becomes 'In the File menu, click Save.'

figures.shows: Eight shuffled step cards for a router reset.
figures.learnerAction: Order the steps and put prerequisites first.

questionPlan.sample: 'Open Settings, select Network, and click Reset.' How many steps should this be?
Which wording follows 'location first'?
choices: Click Save in the File menu.
In the File menu, click Save.
Save is in the File menu, click it.
questionPlan.answer: In the File menu, click Save.

questionPlan.sample: After 'Click Deploy', which addition helps the reader most?
choices: The status changes to Running within 30 seconds.
questionPlan.answer: The status changes to Running within 30 seconds.

lessons.title: Examples and code samples
lessons.objective: Write a minimal, runnable code sample with realistic names, shown output and a one-line explanation.

concepts.title: Minimal sample
concepts.summary: A sample with only what the point needs, small enough to read in one glance.

concepts.title: Runnable sample
concepts.summary: A sample that works when copied, including imports and setup, tested at each release.

concepts.title: Show the output
concepts.summary: Giving the result next to the code lets the reader check their run against it.

misconceptions: Learners put real secrets or placeholders like foo/bar everywhere; use names that tell the reader what the value is, such as YOUR_API_KEY.
Learners explain each line in comments; explain the idea once and let the code show the rest.
sequence: Show a 40-line sample that makes one point.
Trim to the lines that matter.
Make it complete: imports, setup, placeholder values labelled.
Show the output.
Test every sample automatically.
examples: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY' https://api.example.com/v1/items, followed by the JSON the call returns.
A Python sample that uses json without importing it fails at line 1 of use, and a reader will blame themselves.

figures.shows: A short runnable Python sample with its output beside it.
figures.learnerAction: Run the sample and change one value.

questionPlan.sample: data = json.loads('{"a": 1}'); print(data['a']). What is missing for this to run as a standalone sample?
A sample teaches how to set a timeout. Which line is least relevant?
choices: import logging for an unrelated feature
questionPlan.answer: import logging for an unrelated feature

questionPlan.sample: A value such as YOUR_API_KEY that the reader must replace is called a ___.

lessons.title: Reference pages
lessons.objective: Write a reference entry to a fixed template covering name, purpose, parameters, returns, errors and an example.

concepts.title: Reference template
concepts.summary: Every entry has the same fields in the same order so readers can find a detail without reading.

concepts.title: Parameter description
concepts.summary: Each parameter gets a name, type, whether it is required, default and one-sentence description.

concepts.title: Neutral description
concepts.summary: Reference states what is, without instruction or opinion.

misconceptions: Learners write prose paragraphs for reference; a lookup reader needs a table.
Learners omit defaults because 'it is obvious'; the default is often the very thing the reader looks up.
sequence: A reader looking for 'what happens if I leave retries out'.
The fixed template.
Writing one parameter row with unit and default.
Consistency across entries.
Link from reference to how-to and explanation instead of copying.
examples: retries | integer | no | 3 | The number of times a failed request is retried before an error is raised.
timeout | number | no | 30 | The number of seconds to wait for a response.

figures.shows: A reference table for a function with one column missing.

questionPlan.sample: A parameter row lists name, type and description only. Which fields would a reader most need added?
Which description is best for timeout?
choices: The number of seconds to wait for a response before the request fails.
questionPlan.answer: The number of seconds to wait for a response before the request fails.

questionPlan.sample: The value a parameter takes when the reader does not set it is its ___.

lessons.title: Documenting an HTTP API
lessons.objective: Document one endpoint with method, path, authentication, request, response and error cases, using the right status codes.

concepts.title: Endpoint
concepts.summary: An HTTP method and path that performs one operation, such as GET /v1/items/{id}.

concepts.title: Status code
concepts.summary: The three-digit number in a response: 2xx success, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

concepts.title: OpenAPI description
concepts.summary: A machine-readable file describing endpoints, parameters and schemas from which reference pages can be generated.

misconceptions: Learners document only the success case; the error responses are what a reader needs when something goes wrong.
Learners treat 401 and 403 as the same; 401 means the request lacks valid credentials, 403 means the credentials are valid but not permitted.
sequence: One endpoint, the information a reader needs: what it does, method and path, auth, parameters, request body, response body, errors, an example.
A generated reference from an OpenAPI file and why the prose around it is still needed.
Error format: code, message, how to fix.
Rate limits and pagination, documented once.
examples: POST /v1/items creates an item and returns 201 Created with the new item; a missing name returns 400; an expired key returns 401; a key without write permission returns 403; too many calls return 429.
GET /v1/items/{id} for an id that does not exist returns 404 Not Found.

figures.shows: An endpoint page template with rows for method, path, auth, parameters, responses.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the responses row for a given scenario.

figures.shows: A request and response pair drawn as two boxes, with the status line highlighted.

questionPlan.sample: What status code means the client has sent too many requests?
What status code does a successful POST that creates a resource usually return?
A valid key without permission to delete an item calls DELETE. Which status fits?

lessons.title: Docs as code and review
lessons.objective: Keep documentation in version control with a style guide, linting, review and a changelog.

concepts.title: Docs as code
concepts.summary: Writing documentation in plain text files, reviewed and published with the same tools as code.

concepts.title: Style guide
concepts.summary: Agreed rules for terms, tone and formatting, ideally checked by a linter.

concepts.title: Changelog
concepts.summary: A dated list of changes per release, grouped as added, changed, deprecated, removed, fixed and security.

misconceptions: Learners think a changelog is a copy of the commit log; it is written for users and says what changed for them.
Learners treat review as proofreading; a doc review tests whether the steps work.
sequence: Markdown and version control.
A style guide and a linter.
Review checklist: audience, accuracy, steps tested, links.
Versioning docs against product versions.
Changelog categories.
examples: Changelog entry: '### Removed — The v1 /items endpoint. Use /v2/items.'
A review that runs every command in a how-to catches a missing flag that proofreading would not.

figures.shows: A changelog excerpt with category headings.

questionPlan.sample: A release removes an endpoint. Under which Keep a Changelog heading does it go?
Which review check catches a missing flag in a command?
A tool that automatically checks text against a style guide is called a ___.

lessons.title: Testing documentation with readers
lessons.objective: Plan a documentation test with a reader, compute a task success rate, and decide what to fix first.

concepts.title: Documentation usability test
concepts.summary: A reader attempts a real task using only the page while an observer watches without helping.

concepts.title: Task success rate
concepts.summary: Participants who finish the task divided by participants who attempted it.

concepts.title: Feedback loop
concepts.summary: Page ratings, search terms and support tickets that show where docs fail after release.

misconceptions: Learners ask readers if the page is clear; observe whether they finish.
Learners treat low page views as proof a page is unneeded; a page may be unfindable.
sequence: Pick one task and one page.
Recruit someone who matches the audience statement.
Watch silently, note where they stop.
Success rate and the first point of failure.
Fix the failure that stops most readers first.
examples: 8 of 10 testers finish the install: 80% success; 2 stopped at step 4 because it assumed a tool was installed.
Support gets 30 tickets a month on one error not covered in the troubleshooting page: add it there.

figures.shows: A funnel across steps 1–8 with the drop at step 4 highlighted.
figures.learnerAction: Click a step to see how many readers stopped.

questionPlan.sample: 8 of 10 testers finish a task. What is the success rate as a percentage?
6 testers stop at step 4 and 1 stops at step 7. Which fix first?
Recall: why does a test with a real reader find faults that proofreading misses?
questionPlan.answer: The reader follows the page without the author's knowledge, so skipped steps and unclear terms stop them.

courseCheck: A mixed check: write an audience statement; classify a page as tutorial, how-to, reference or explanation; choose a list type; rewrite a passive sentence; compute a Flesch score and a percentage cut; split a compound step; find a missing reference field; pick a status code; choose a changelog category; compute a task success rate. One short self-rated recall on the four editing passes.
